title: Measuring surprise
objectives: Compute a $z$ statistic for a sample mean.

screens.title: Which average is stranger?
screens.prose: Two records, each judged against a no-skill mean of 0. Strategy A averaged 0.3% a day over 100 days. Fund B averaged 2% a month over 12 months. The table gives the sd of one period.
screens.question: If neither had any skill, which average would be more surprising?

options.text: A’s 0.3%, though it is the smaller number
B’s 2%, because it is the bigger number
options.why: You compared the raw averages. B’s luck is far wider: $5\%/\sqrt{12} \approx 1.44\%$, against A’s $1\%/\sqrt{100} = 0.1\%$.

options.text: Equally surprising, since both are above 0
options.why: Being above 0 is not enough. What matters is how far above, measured in each record’s own noise.

options.text: They cannot be compared: days and months differ
options.why: They can, once each average is measured in units of its own standard error.

hints.text: How far could luck move each average? Use the standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$.
A’s standard error is $1\%/\sqrt{100} = 0.1\%$. B’s is $5\%/\sqrt{12} \approx 1.44\%$.
A sits $0.3/0.1 = 3$ standard errors above 0. B sits $2/1.44 \approx 1.39$.

feedback.correct: A sits 3 standard errors above 0; B only about 1.4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Measure each average against the luck it could contain.

explain.text: A’s average is 3 standard errors above 0, while B’s is about 1.39. Luck reaches 1.39 standard errors often and 3 rarely. To compare surprise, count standard errors.

screens.title: Counting standard errors
screens.prose: A strategy with no skill has true mean $\mu_0 = 0$ and daily sd $\sigma = 1\%$. Over $n = 100$ days its average $\bar X$ is close to normal, with standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n = 0.1\%$. Slide the observed average $\bar x$.
screens.question: Slide until the shaded tail is just under 0.025. How many standard errors above $\mu_0$ is $\bar x$?

widget.label: Standard errors above the null mean
widget.accept: about 2 (1.95 to 2.05). At $\bar x = 0.20\%$ the tail is 0.0228; the exact cut-off is 1.96.

hints.text: Watch the tail label above the curve as you slide.
The caption counts the standard errors for you.
At $\bar x = 0.20\%$ the tail is 0.0228, just under 0.025. Read the count in the caption.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Stop where the tail first drops below 0.025, then read the caption.

byKey.xbar: You gave $\bar x$ itself, in percent. The question asks how many standard errors that is.
byKey.tail: That is the tail chance. The question asks for the count of standard errors in the caption.

explain.text: The tail first drops below 0.025 at $\bar x = 0.20\%$, two standard errors above 0. The exact cut-off is 1.96 standard errors. Counting standard errors puts every average on one scale.

screens.title: The z statistic
screens.prose: The count you read is the **$z$ statistic**: how many standard errors the observed average sits from the null mean. $$z = \frac{\bar x - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$$ A second strategy averaged $\bar x = 0.25\%$ over $n = 64$ days, with known $\sigma = 1\%$ and $H_0: \mu = 0$.
screens.question: What is $z$?

hints.text: Find the standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$ first.
The shaded tail starts at $\bar x = 0.25$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide $\bar x - \mu_0$ by $\sigma/\sqrt n$.

byKey.sigma: You divided by $\sigma = 1\%$, the noise of one day. Divide by the standard error of the 64-day average.
byKey.over-n: You divided by $\sigma/n$. Averaging shrinks the noise by $\sqrt n$, not by $n$.
byKey.times-root: You divided by $\sigma\sqrt n$. The standard error is $\sigma$ divided by $\sqrt n$.

explain.text: The standard error is $1\%/8 = 0.125\%$. So $\bar x = 0.25\%$ is $z = 2$ standard errors above $\mu_0 = 0$. The tail beyond it has chance 0.0228.

screens.title: A null mean that is not zero
screens.prose: An execution algorithm used to slip $\mu_0 = 2.0$ basis points (bp) per order, with $\sigma = 6$ bp. After a change we average $n = 144$ orders. Under $H_0$ nothing changed.
screens.question: Slide $\bar x$ to the value that gives $z = -1.96$.

hints.text: Find the standard error first: $6/\sqrt{144}$.
The curve is centred on $\mu_0 = 2.0$, not on 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Go 1.96 standard errors below the null mean of 2.0.

byKey.above: You went 1.96 standard errors above the null mean. A negative $z$ sits below it.
byKey.one-se: That is one standard error below 2.0. Go 1.96 of them.

explain.text: The standard error is $6/12 = 0.5$ bp. So $z = -1.96$ sits at $\bar x = 2.0 - 0.98 = 1.02$ bp. An average below that would be surprising at 5% if nothing had changed.

screens.title: Surprising at 5%
screens.prose: Under $H_0$, $z$ is close to $N(0, 1)$ whatever the test. The middle 95% lies between $-1.96$ and $1.96$. A two-sided result outside it is called **surprising at 5%**.
screens.question: Which results are surprising at 5%, two-sided? Select all that apply.

options.why: You counted 1.90 as surprising. It is close to 1.96, but still inside.
You counted −1.50. It sits well inside the middle 95%.
You counted 0.08. It is almost exactly at the centre.

hints.text: Compare the size of each $z$ with 1.96, ignoring its sign.
Surprising values lie outside the shaded middle.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick exactly the values with $|z| > 1.96$.

explain.text: Your picks are the values with $|z| > 1.96$: 2.30, −2.10 and 3.00. The value 1.90 falls just inside. Two-sided means the sign does not matter, only the size.

screens.title: Noise of a day, noise of an average
screens.prose: A strategy averaged $\bar x = 0.15\%$ a day over $n = 400$ days, with known $\sigma = 1.2\%$ and $H_0: \mu = 0$. A colleague computes $0.15/1.2 = 0.125$ and calls it noise.

state.caption: The null curve for a 400-day average

screens.question: What is the correct $z$?

hints.text: Is $\sigma = 1.2\%$ the noise of one day or of the 400-day average?
Read the width of the null curve: far narrower than 1.2%.
The standard error is $1.2\%/\sqrt{400} = 0.06\%$. Divide 0.15 by it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide by the standard error of the average, $\sigma/\sqrt n$.

byKey.sigma: You divided by $\sigma$, the noise of a single day, as your colleague did. A 400-day average is 20 times less noisy.
byKey.over-n: You divided by $\sigma/n$. Averaging shrinks the noise by $\sqrt{400} = 20$, not by 400.
byKey.centre: You centred the curve on $\bar x$, so $\bar x$ sat 0 errors from itself. Centre on the null mean, $\mu_0 = 0$.

explain.text: The 400-day average has standard error $1.2\%/20 = 0.06\%$. So $z = 0.15/0.06 = 2.5$, well past 1.96. Dividing by $\sigma$ judged the average as if it were a single day.

screens.title: Why one cut-off serves every test
screens.prose: Daily returns $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ are independent, each with mean $\mu$ and known sd $\sigma$. We test $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$. Put the steps in order.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: Under $H_0$, $E[\bar X] = \mu_0$, by linearity of expectation
$\text{Var}(\bar X) = \sigma^2/n$: independent variances add, and $\bar X$ divides the sum by $n$
By the central limit theorem, $\bar X$ is close to $N(\mu_0, \sigma^2/n)$
Standardise: $Z = \dfrac{\bar X - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$ is close to $N(0, 1)$

hints.text: Start with the centre and the spread of $\bar X$.
The central limit theorem needs the mean and the variance first.
Mean, variance, central limit theorem, standardise, then the 1.96 cut-off.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build the null distribution of $\bar X$ before you standardise it.

byKey.s4: Standardising gives $N(0, 1)$ only once the central limit theorem has made $\bar X$ normal.
byKey.s5: The cut-off comes last, once $Z$ is standard normal.

explain.text: Subtracting $\mu_0$ and dividing by $\sigma/\sqrt n$ turns every such $\bar X$ into the same $N(0, 1)$. So one cut-off, 1.96, serves every test of a mean. Only the standard error changes from test to test.

screens.title: A year of a strategy
screens.prose: A strategy’s backtest shows a mean daily return of 0.08% over 250 days. Its daily sd is known from a long history: 1.2%. We test $H_0: \mu = 0$.
screens.question: What is $z$? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: Standard error first: $1.2\%/\sqrt{250}$.
The shaded tail starts at the observed 0.08%.

byKey.sigma: You divided by $\sigma = 1.2\%$, the noise of one day. Use the standard error of the 250-day average.
byKey.over-n: You divided by $\sigma/n$. The standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt n$.
byKey.times-root: You divided by $\sigma\sqrt n$. The standard error divides by $\sqrt n$.

explain.text: The standard error is $1.2\%/\sqrt{250} \approx 0.0759\%$. So $z = 0.08/0.0759 \approx 1.054$, well inside ±1.96. A year of 0.08% a day is not yet surprising for a strategy this noisy.

screens.title: Did the fill rate improve?
screens.prose: An order router filled 60% of orders. After a change, 1,000 orders fill at 63%. Under $H_0: f = 0.60$, each order fills or not, so one order has sd $\sqrt{0.6 \times 0.4}$.
screens.question: What is $z$? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: The standard error of a fill rate is $\sqrt{0.6 \times 0.4/n}$.
The curve is centred on the null rate 0.60.

byKey.phat: You used 0.63 in the standard error. Under $H_0$ the fill chance is 0.60, so the sd uses 0.60.
byKey.no-n: You divided by the sd of one order, $\sqrt{0.24}$. Divide by the standard error of 1,000 orders.

explain.text: Under $H_0$ the standard error is $\sqrt{0.6 \times 0.4/1000} \approx 0.0155$. So $z = 0.03/0.0155 \approx 1.936$, just inside 1.96. The rise is close to surprising at 5%, but not past it.

ideas: Under $H_0$, the sample mean $\bar X$ is close to $N(\mu_0, \sigma^2/n)$: centred on the null mean, with standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$.
The $z$ statistic counts standard errors from the null mean: $z = (\bar x - \mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)$.
Under $H_0$, $z$ is close to $N(0, 1)$, so luck gives $|z| > 1.96$ only 5% of the time.

formula.name: The z statistic
formula.note: For known $\sigma$. With one observation, $n = 1$ and $z = (x - \mu_0)/\sigma$.

summary.trap: Divide by the standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$, not by $\sigma$, and centre on the null mean $\mu_0$, not on $\bar x$.

quiz.prose: A market maker captures £0.50 a trade on average, with known sd £0.40. This week 64 trades averaged £0.41. Test $H_0: \mu = 0.50$.
quiz.question: What is $z$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the null mean, then divide by $0.40/\sqrt{64}$.

byKey.flipped: You subtracted the other way, $\mu_0 - \bar x$. With $\bar x - \mu_0$, a fall gives a negative $z$.
byKey.sigma: You divided by the sd of one trade. Divide by the standard error, $0.40/8 = 0.05$.

explain.text: The standard error is $£0.40/\sqrt{64} = £0.05$. So $z = (0.41 - 0.50)/0.05 = -1.8$. That is inside ±1.96, so not surprising at 5%.

quiz.prose: On ordinary days a stock’s return has mean 0 and known sd 2%. Today it fell 5%. Treat today as a sample of one, $n = 1$.
quiz.question: What is $z$ for today?

widget.label: z statistic
widget.accept: −2.5: with $n = 1$ the standard error is $\sigma$ itself, so $z = -5/2$

byKey.sign: The stock fell, so $x - \mu_0$ is negative.
byKey.percent: You mixed units. Keep both the return and $\sigma$ in percent: $-5/2$.

explain.text: With $n = 1$ the standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt 1 = \sigma$. So $z = (-5 - 0)/2 = -2.5$, a move of 2.5 sds. One day is the smallest sample there is.

quiz.prose: A test gives some $z$. You keep $\bar x$, $\mu_0$ and $\sigma$ the same, but collect four times as many days.
quiz.question: What happens to $z$?

options.text: It is four times as large
options.why: You let $z$ grow with $n$. It grows with $\sqrt n$, and $\sqrt 4 = 2$.
The standard error halves, so $z$, which divides by it, doubles.
The same average from more days is harder to reach by luck, so $z$ must grow.

feedback.correct: The standard error halves, so $z$ doubles.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what four times the days does to $\sigma/\sqrt n$.

explain.text: Quadrupling $n$ halves the standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$. Since $z$ divides by it, $z$ doubles. Evidence grows like $\sqrt n$.

quiz.prose: A two-sided test of a mean gives $z = -2.4$.
quiz.question: Is the result surprising at 5%?

options.text: No: a negative $z$ is never surprising
options.why: You looked at the sign. A two-sided test counts large values in either direction.

options.text: Only if the test were one-sided
options.why: You have it the wrong way round. Two-sided tests count the low tail too.
$\sigma$ is already inside $z$. The cut-off 1.96 works for any $\sigma$.

explain.text: A two-sided test asks whether $|z| > 1.96$. Here $|z| = 2.4$, so luck alone would rarely give it. The minus sign only says the average fell below $\mu_0$.
